independence.prior_role: Unit6 grammar/source-form auditor; neither master authored
independence.key_access: Only after explicit coordinator phase2 authorization
independence.method: Manual full key/learner/solution comparison plus separately reconstructed source-based models; structural checks are not substituted for linguistic inspection.

text_identity_checks.printed_text: Ic cann swimman. Hē mæg ðæt wæter beran.
text_identity_checks.manual_linguistic_review: Learned cunnan + swimman is distinguished from capability mugan + beran; the water object and singular agreement are correct.
Sculon with plain gefręmman expresses obligation; prior work-object frame is actually productive.
Wolde with plain faran expresses past desire to travel, not accomplished travel; ordinary intransitive frame is explicitly new.

text_identity_checks.printed_text: Nim ðone męte. Nimað ðone męte.
text_identity_checks.manual_linguistic_review: Singular versus plural taking/carrying commands preserve the singular masculine food object and hine reference.

text_identity_checks.printed_text: Gief mē ðæt wæter. Helpað mē.
text_identity_checks.manual_linguistic_review: Plural helping and giving commands preserve the prior dative mē recipient/person-helped frame and accusative water.
Ne drinc is an ordinary singular prohibition with the learned drink-water frame; ne negates the command without an auxiliary.
Cōm tō helpanne has the same arriving/helper subject and dative helped person; purpose does not imply fulfillment.
Cōm tō giefanne preserves accusative gift and dative bird recipients inside the infinitive.
Bið with strong nominative neuter gearu is sound in the expressly expected-later setting; no blanket future-only rule.
Wāt with accusative ðā ðing uses the explicitly new known-fact/matter sense, supported by nominal witan and BT’s þing example.

text_identity_checks.printed_text: Se mann cwæð: ‘Ic wille faran. Mīn scip is gearu. Cumað and helpað mē.’ Twēgen gefēran cōmon tō helpanne. Se mann cwæð: ‘Nimað ðone męte and berað hine. Giefað ðǣm fuglum ðæt wæter.’ Se gefēra cwæð: ‘Ic mæg ðone męte beran. Wē sculon ðæt weorc gefręmman.’ Ðā gefēran bǣron ðone męte and gēafon ðǣm fuglum ðæt wæter. Se mann cwæð: ‘Sittað and etað.’ Ðā gefēran ǣton. Hīe fōron.
text_identity_checks.manual_linguistic_review: All 68 tokens, 7 imperative occurrences and finite/infinitive dependencies checked against actual earlier registers and selected new models. Translation independently prepared in C5 before key access; compare C1–C6 for semantic/reference checks.

text_identity_checks.printed_text: Ðā, sōna swā se fiscere geseah ðæt se geonga mann æt his fōtum læg, hē mid mildheortnesse hine ūpāhōf, and lǣdde hine mid him tō his hūse, and ðā ēstas him beforan lęgde ðe hē him tō bēodanne hæfde. Ðā gīet hē wolde, be his mihte, māran ārfæstnesse him gecȳðan; tōslāt ðā his wǣfels on twā, and sealde Apollonie ðone healfan dǣl, ðus cweðende: “Nim ðæt ic ðē tō sęllanne hæbbe, and gā intō ðǣre ceastre.”
text_identity_checks.manual_linguistic_review: All 76 source tokens checked against the retained p167/PDF183 image and independent R8 translation. Exact words and quantities retained; only declared line/quote/note-cue presentation normalization. Ten supports close the extra lexical and syntactic demands.

review_stage: Phase2: full learner/key/source/dependency review, before exports

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give all six person-and-number cells of the present indicative and all six of the preterite indicative of witan. Use the selected course forms and label every cell even where spellings coincide.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All twelve witan cells agree: wāt/wāst/witon against wiste/wistest/wiston. Present knowledge is distinguished from historical strong-past shape.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give all six person-and-number cells of the present indicative and all six of the preterite indicative of cunnan. Use the selected course forms and label every cell even where spellings coincide.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All twelve cunnan cells agree. Cann/canst/cunnon and cūðe/cūðest/cūðon preserve singular/plural stem contrast and long ū in the dental past.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give all six person-and-number cells of the present indicative and all six of the preterite indicative of ðurfan. Use the selected course forms and label every cell even where spellings coincide.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All twelve ðurfan cells agree: ðearf-/ðurf- present, ðorft- past, including ðearft and ðorftest. Need is the stated construction.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give all six person-and-number cells of the present indicative and all six of the preterite indicative of durran. Use the selected course forms and label every cell even where spellings coincide.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All twelve durran cells agree, including present dearr/dearst/durron and past dorste/dorstest/dorston. No fictive ordinary command or infinitive is required.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give all six person-and-number cells of the present indicative and all six of the preterite indicative of sculan. Use the selected course forms and label every cell even where spellings coincide.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All twelve sculan cells agree: sceal/scealt/sculon, sceolde/sceoldest/sceoldon. Scolde-series is fairly distinguished as a documented nonselected alternative.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give all six person-and-number cells of the present indicative and all six of the preterite indicative of mugan. Use the selected course forms and label every cell even where spellings coincide.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All twelve mugan/magan cells agree: mæg/meaht/magon, meahte/meahtest/meahton. Conventional lemma spelling is not used as proof of an infinitive.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give all six person-and-number cells of the present indicative and all six of the preterite indicative of mōtan. Use the selected course forms and label every cell even where spellings coincide.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All twelve mōtan cells agree, including second-singular mōst versus mōstest and long ō throughout the selected system.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give all six person-and-number cells of the present indicative and all six of the preterite indicative of dōn. Use the selected course forms and label every cell even where spellings coincide.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All twelve dōn cells agree. Dō/dēst/dēð/dōð and dyde/dydest/dydon are kept separate from command dō.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give all six person-and-number cells of the present indicative and all six of the preterite indicative of gān. Use the selected course forms and label every cell even where spellings coincide.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All twelve gān cells agree. Gǣst/gǣð have long ǣ; gā/gāð have long ā; ēod- is the separate preterite stem.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give all six person-and-number cells of the present indicative and all six of the preterite indicative of willan. Use the selected course forms and label every cell even where spellings coincide.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All twelve willan cells agree. Both first- and third-singular present select wille, second singular wilt, plural willað; past wolde/woldest/woldon.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give all six person-and-number cells of the bēo present indicative series. Then give the corresponding earlier eom series. Does bēo supply a separate past-tense paradigm?
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All six bēo-series and six earlier eom-series cells agree; no independent bēon preterite is invented. The earlier wæs/wǣre/wǣron system remains the past.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Compare wāt and wiste; cann and cūðe; gǣð and ēode; dēð and dyde. Using a third-person singular subject, identify the tense of each. Which forms can also serve a first-person singular subject? Explain why wāt and cann are not translated as past-tense forms.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All eight form/tense/person comparisons agree. Gǣð and dēð alone are not first-singular indicative; the six remaining comparison forms are syncretic first/third singular in the specified tense.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: The reference notes mark some modal infinitive citations as unattested or uncertain. Explain why a dictionary label such as mugan does not authorize you to create an infinitive or a command for every modal verb. Distinguish a missing paradigm cell from two attested cells with the same spelling.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Key and solution distinguish unattested citation labels from genuine syncretism, and avoid generating modal infinitives or regular command pairs. Documented command functions/subjunctive substitutes are acknowledged, not denied.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “I know how to swim. We know how to sing.” Use cunnan for learned ability.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Cann/cunnon plus plain swimman/singan expresses learned ability. Both subjects and tense are correct; no prior citation exposure is treated as prior infinitival use.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “He can carry the water. They can help the man.” Use mugan for ability.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Mæg/magon plus plain beran/helpan is correct. Water is accusative; ðǣm męnn is dative under the actual prior helpan frame.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “I need to go. We needed to go.” Use ðurfan.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Ic ðearf gān and Wē ðorfton gān correctly contrast present need with actual past need. Plain gān is unchanged.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “You dare to go. You dared to go.” Address one person and use durran.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Ðū dearst gān and Ðū dorstest gān correctly preserve singular address and present/past daring.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “We must do the work. They had to do the work.” Use sculan for obligation.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Sculon/sceoldon with plain dōn and accusative ðæt weorc express present/past obligation, not accomplished action or automatically hypothetical would.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “You are allowed to eat the food. You were allowed to eat the food.” Address one person and use mōtan.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Mōst/mōstest express the explicitly requested present/past permission, with etan and accusative food. Obligation is not substituted for permission.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “He wants to give the birds water. They wanted to give the birds water.” Use willan for desire.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Wille/woldon with plain giefan and dative bird recipients preserve desire; water is accusative. Sęllan is a defensible taught alternative without asserting that the giving occurred.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “I did not dare to go. We cannot carry the ship.” Use the taught simple ne construction.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Simple ne negates finite dorste/magon in the taught bounded constructions. Gān/beran remain plain; no new contracted negative system is required.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “We two know how to swim. You two must help us two.” Keep the two-person references.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Wit/git take plural cunnon/sculon; unc is dative under helpan. Both two-person references remain explicit.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “He wanted to go. He went.” Explain why the first sentence alone does not assert that he went.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: The key model wolde gān / ēode and the independently written wolde faran / fōr both satisfy the unrestricted go prompt. The key rubric permits defensible wording; intention is distinguished from actual travel.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate the printed pairs Ic cann swimman and Ic mæg swimman using the unit’s stated difference between learned ability and present capability. Identify the finite verb and the infinitive in each. Do not claim that one English word always represents only one Old English modal.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: The selected learned-skill versus present-capability contrast is explained without a false universal one-English-word rule; cann/mæg are finite, swimman infinitival.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “The ship will be ready.” Use the bēo-series indicative to describe the expected later state. Then contrast the earlier eom-series sentence “The ship is ready.” Do not infer that every bēo-series occurrence must be future.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Ðæt scip bið gearu versus ... is gearu meets the explicitly later context and requested series. Strong nominative neuter gearu is appropriate in the predicate despite the subject article.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: The “things” here are matters already discussed. Translate “I know those things. He knew those things.” Use witan. Explain how this knowledge construction differs from cunnan followed by an infinitive.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Ic wāt ðā ðing / Hē wiste ðā ðing uses the explicitly new fact/matter sense and accusative nominal-object frame. It is properly contrasted with knowing-how plus an infinitive.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the second-person singular and plural imperatives of hīeran, nęrian and gefręmman. Label both numbers.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All three pairs agree: hīer/hīerað, nęre/nęriað, gefręme/gefręmmað; final-e retention and restoration of plural stem material are explained.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the second-person singular and plural imperatives of cyssan, gefyllan, sęttan, gierwan and sęllan. Label both numbers.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All five pairs agree: cys/cyssað, gefyl/gefyllað, sęte/sęttað, giere/gierwað, sęle/sęllað. Heavy final-geminate simplification is separated from short-stem -e and -w behavior.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the second-person singular and plural imperatives of lufian, habban and libban. Label both numbers.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All three pairs agree: lufa/lufiað, hafa/habbað, leofa/libbað; weak-II -a/-iað and weak-III irregular stems are explicit.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the second-person singular and plural imperatives of sęcgan and hycgan. Label both numbers.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Both pairs agree: saga/sęcgað and hoga/hycgað. Sęge is a documented alternative to selected saga; an ordinary weak-I derivation is not imposed.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the second-person singular and plural imperatives of drīfan, bēodan, bindan, helpan and drincan. Label both numbers.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All five strong pairs agree: drīf/drīfað, bēod/bēodað, bind/bindað, help/helpað, drinc/drincað. Quantities and plural -að are preserved.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the second-person singular and plural imperatives of wrēon and tēon. Label both numbers.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Wrīh/wrēoð and tēoh/tēoð agree; contraction is not handled by mechanically dropping infinitive -n.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the second-person singular and plural imperatives of beran, niman and cuman. Label both numbers.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Ber/berað, nim/nimað and cum/cumað agree. Cuman has cum- in both command cells.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the second-person singular and plural imperatives of giefan, biddan, sittan, licgan and etan. Label both numbers.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Gief/giefað, bide/biddað, site/sittað, lige/licgað and et/etað agree. The j-present singular -e and plural consonants are preserved.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the second-person singular and plural imperatives of sēon, slēan and fōn. Label both numbers.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Seoh/sēoð, sleah/slēað and fōh/fōð agree. The first two singular diphthongs are unmarked short in the selected sources, unlike their long contracted plurals.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the second-person singular and plural imperatives of hębban, scieppan and swęrian. Label both numbers.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Hęfe/hębbað, sciepe/scieppað and swęre/swęriað agree, including hooked e and the retained plural -iað of swęrian.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the second-person singular and plural imperatives of faran, standan and healdan. Label both numbers.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Far/farað, stand/standað and heald/healdað agree. Standan retains the nasal in the command, not its preterite stem.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the second-person singular and plural imperatives of weaxan, hātan and lǣtan. Label both numbers.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Weax/weaxað, hāt/hātað and lǣt/lǣtað agree; both marked long vowels are retained.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the second-person singular and plural imperatives of dōn, gān and both command series of wesan/bēon. Label both numbers.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All four pairs agree: dō/dōð, gā/gāð, wes/wesað and bēo/bēoð. These are second-person commands; no willan command pair is invented.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “Take the food and carry it.” First address one person, then several. Identify what “it” refers to and preserve its grammatical gender.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Both number versions of take/carry are correct. Hine is masculine accusative singular for food; plural addressees do not pluralize the object.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “Help me. Give me the water.” First address one person, then exactly two people. Explain the verb number used for the two addressees.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Help/gief versus helpað/giefað correctly addresses one versus exactly two. Mē is dative with each verb; no dual imperative ending is invented. Taught sęllan can express the same giving frame.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “Do not drink the water. Sit and eat.” Address several people.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Ne drincað, sittað and etað are plural commands. Prior drinking-water and objectless-eating frames and new ordinary negative command scope cover the entire answer.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “The man said: ‘Go and do the work well.’” The man addresses one companion.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Cwæð introduces a past report of direct speech; gā/dō stay singular imperatives. Work is accusative and wel modifies the doing. Quotation is not converted to an indirect mood construction.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the plain infinitive and the selected inflected infinitive after tō for bindan, beran and sęllan. Use the course’s -anne forms where the table selects them.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All three pairs agree: bindan/bindanne, beran/beranne, sęllan/sęllanne after tō; gemination in the infinitive is retained.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the plain infinitive and the selected inflected infinitive after tō for hīeran, cyssan, nęrian, gefręmman and gierwan. Use the course’s -anne forms where the table selects them.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All five pairs agree: hīeran/hīeranne, cyssan/cyssanne, nęrian/nęrianne, gefręmman/gefręmmanne, gierwan/gierwanne. Infinitive stems do not inherit singular-command reductions.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the plain infinitive and the selected inflected infinitive after tō for lufian, habban, libban, sęcgan and hycgan. Use the course’s -anne forms where the table selects them.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All five pairs agree: lufian/lufianne, habban/habbanne, libban/libbanne, sęcgan/sęcganne, hycgan/hycganne. Weak-III command stem alternations are not imported into infinitives.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the plain infinitive and the selected inflected infinitive after tō for wrēon, tēon, sēon, slēan and fōn. Use the course’s -anne forms where the table selects them.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All five contracted pairs agree: wrēon/wrēonne, tēon/tēonne, sēon/sēonne, slēan/slēanne, fōn/fōnne. The contracted -n to -nne rule is correctly distinguished.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Give the plain infinitive and the selected inflected infinitive after tō for gān, dōn and both wesan/bēon series. Use the course’s -anne forms where the table selects them.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All four pairs agree: gān/gānne, dōn/dōnne, wesan/wesanne, bēon/bēonne. No unlicensed modal citations enter the answer.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “He wants to eat. He came to eat.” Use the taught plain-infinitive complement in the first sentence and the taught purpose construction in the second.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Wille etan expresses desire; cōm tō etanne gives the arriving subject’s purpose. The latter is not an assertion that eating occurred.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “The companions came to help the man.” Use the inflected infinitive for their purpose. Identify the person doing the helping and the case of the person helped.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Companions are the plural cōmon subject and intended helpers; tō helpanne preserves dative ðǣm męnn as the person helped.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “The man came to give food to the birds.” Use the inflected infinitive for the purpose.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Cōm tō giefanne with accusative męte and dative birds is correct. The independent solution places gift before recipient, while the key reverses them; both orders preserve the same taught relations.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: In Hīe sculon ðæt weorc dōn and Hīe cōmon tō dōnne ðæt weorc, identify each finite verb, each infinitive, and the construction that selects the infinitive form. Translate both sentences.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Sculon + dōn expresses obligation; cōmon + tō dōnne expresses same-subject purpose. Finite tense and number are correctly separated from nonfinite shape.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Complete the taught modal construction “We can carry the food” using mugan and beran. Then make the subject “I”. Explain which verb changes for person and number.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Wē magon ... beran changes to Ic mæg ... beran. Only the finite modal changes for the subject; beran and accusative food remain the same.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Read “Food and water for the journey”. Who asks for help, how many companions come, and what is their stated purpose? Answer in English.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: The man asks for help, two companions come, and their explicit purpose is to help him. No commanded act is mistaken for a completed past event.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: List every imperative in the controlled text and give its addressee number. For each, give the singular command form taught in the tables.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: All seven plural command tokens are listed: cumað, helpað, nimað, berað, giefað, sittað, etað; the corresponding singulars cum, help, nim, ber, gief, site, et all agree.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: In the controlled text, identify the antecedent and case of hine, the recipient of the water, and what the companions subsequently eat. Distinguish what is explicit from what the context suggests.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Hine is masculine accusative singular referring to męte. Mē identifies the man as water recipient; ðone męte gives the food later eaten. Context supports companions as final hīe without making inclusive reference grammatically impossible.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Identify wille, mæg and sculon in the controlled text by person, number, tense and stated sense. Give the infinitive governed by each.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Wille is first-singular present desire with faran, mæg first-singular present ability with beran, sculon first-plural present obligation with gefręmman. All agree with the direct-speech subjects.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate the whole controlled text. Preserve the distinctions among a wish to travel, ability to carry, obligation, commands and completed past actions.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Both full 68-word translations preserve intention, capability, obligation, plural commands, completed arrival/carrying/sitting/eating/travel and reference. Natural English wording differs without changing the relations.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Rewrite the man’s first quoted commands, Cumað and helpað mē, as commands to one companion. Separately, put the first sentence of the original narrative into the present, keeping its original quotation unchanged.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Original prompt admits two readings of unchanged quotation; both were frozen in the independent solution. Actual amended prompt now explicitly applies the present-tense operation to the original narrative. Key cum/help and cwið with original Cumað/helpað quotation now fit the task unambiguously.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Read “The fisherman’s gift and first direction”, using its local support. What prompts the fisherman’s action, what does he divide, and what does he give Apollonius?
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Supported answer correctly identifies the young man lying at the fisherman’s feet, division of the fisherman’s cloak and gift of one half to Apollonius.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Find wolde and its plain infinitive in the source. Parse wolde and explain the fisherman’s intention. Use the supplied meaning of gecȳðan.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Wolde is third-singular preterite volition governing supplied plain gecȳðan; the fisherman wishes to show greater kindness according to his means.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Identify tō bēodanne and tō sęllanne. Give the familiar plain infinitive behind each. Explain the source’s “have to offer/give” phrases using the printed support; do not translate them as modern English “must”.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Bēodanne/sęllanne are selected inflected infinitives after tō, corresponding to bēodan/sęllan. The local habban construction describes something available to offer/give, not obligation.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Find the source’s two singular commands. Parse each and give its plural command form from the taught system.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Nim and gā are singular imperatives; their learned plurals nimað and gāð agree. No source-local material is needed for unscaffolded recall.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Use the notes to distinguish the participial cweðende from the finite past cwæð and the command gā. Which form introduces the fisherman’s actual words?
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Supplied cweðende is an accompanying present participle introducing speech; cwæð is finite preterite and gā a command. Appearance in the source does not promote participial syntax.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: What does the fisherman say he has, and what first direction does he give? Explain the force of the phrase translated “what I have” using the local support.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: The speaker has something available to give and directs Apollonius into the town. Definite free-relative what/that which is supplied as a whole; the key does not claim a uniquely identifiable mood from hæbbe alone.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Identify the source’s tō phrases that contain an inflected infinitive and distinguish them from tō his hūse and intō ðǣre ceastre. State the locally supplied meanings of the destination phrases without deriving a general motion-preposition rule.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Tō bēodanne and tō sęllanne are infinitival. Tō his hūse and intō ðǣre ceastre are supplied destination phrases with actual dative forms, despite motion. No general accusative-motion rule is inferred.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate the whole 76-word source excerpt with its supports. Stop after the fisherman’s first direction; do not add the continuation of his speech.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: The complete source translation preserves the fisherman/Apollonius references, food, available-to-offer construction, intention, cloak division, gift, participial speech introduction and first direction. It stops after ceastre and does not import the continuing source speech.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “We two wanted to give our food to the birds. We two gave it to them.” Retain the two-person possessor and the grammatical gender of “food”.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Wit woldon ... uncerne męte ... and Wit gēafon ... preserve dual subject/possessor, masculine accusative food, dative birds and masculine hine. Key and independent solution differ only in a defensible order of the two object pronouns.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “The old man cannot carry the great ship. Help him.” Address several companions in the command.
task_reviews.manual_comparison: Weak ealda/micle occur under the selected noun-phrase determiners; ne mæg ... beran denies capability; plural helpað governs dative him. All adjective and case dependencies are actually productive earlier.

task_reviews.actual_prompt: Translate “He came to help us. We wanted to give him food. He sat and ate.” Use the taught elementary purpose and volitional constructions.
